chunks: "Soldermask is the thin polymer coating on the outside of a PCB, usually green, that covers the copper everywhere except the pads and other places you want exposed.
It's an epoxy-based film about 20 to 30 microns thick, normally applied as a liquid, exposed with UV through the pattern, developed to open the pads, and cured.
During soldering it acts as a barrier so solder only sticks to the pads, which stops bridges between fine-pitch pins and keeps solder from running along traces.
It protects the copper from oxidation, corrosion, moisture and contamination.
It insulates the traces from accidental shorts, for example from a dropped screwdriver or a metal enclosure. And it gives a bit of mechanical protection from scratches.

For layout, you define the opening around each pad, a bit larger than the pad to allow for registration error, say 50 microns per side, and you keep a minimum strip of mask, a solder dam, between pads, typically 0.
1 millimetres or more depending on the fab. You can have pads defined by the copper, NSMD, which is common for BGAs, or by the mask, SMD.
Vias are usually tented, covered with mask, to keep solder out.
It's different from solder paste, which is the solder alloy put onto pads with a stencil, and from the silkscreen, which is the text layer on top."
